title: Geometric Rényi divergence and RLD Fisher information under quantum processes without definite causal order
abstract: Quantum experiments without a definite causal order offer new ways to distinguish devices, estimate physical parameters, and communicate. We prove a common limit on these tasks: the geometric Rényi divergence at the output of a deterministic completely positive process cannot exceed the sum of the divergences of its individual channel uses. The inequality holds for every Rényi order in $(0,1)\cup(1,2]$ and any number of independently replaceable channels. Parallel experiments with separate reference-assisted inputs approach the bound, giving an exact equality after optimization over processes. We also prove an additive bound on the right logarithmic derivative Fisher information of parameter-dependent channels under every fixed process in this class. A resulting Cramér--Rao bound limits locally unbiased estimation precision without assuming a definite causal order, and an erasure-probability example attains the bound. The proofs for the geometric Rényi divergence and RLD Fisher information follow from the requirement that every independent choice of channels produce a normalized output. We show how this requirement controls positive local operations, and how small channel perturbations convert the divergence inequality into a Fisher-information bound, including for singular channels. Further applications give finite-use bounds on channel discrimination and exclusion, together with communication and private-state-generation converses when the processes preserve the relevant comparison conditions.
summary: This paper derives fundamental, additive bounds for quantum information measures—specifically the geometric Rényi divergence and the RLD Fisher information—when quantum processes lack a definite causal order. It shows that the total resource capacity is limited by the sum of the capacities of the individual channels used. This provides a powerful, order-independent tool for analyzing quantum communication and estimation protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to quantify distinguishability, parameter estimation precision, and communication capabilities in quantum experiments where the causal order of multiple channel uses is not fixed.
main_result: It establishes additive bounds for both the geometric Rényi divergence and the RLD Fisher information, showing that the total bound is the sum of the bounds from individual, independently used channels.
method: The analysis derives these bounds by replacing the standard sequential chain rule with a normalization requirement imposed on the output of the overall process, utilizing operator inequalities and divergence definitions.
model_or_system: The model involves general quantum processes acting on Choi operators, which are composed of multiple, independently replaceable quantum channels ($\mathcal{N}_i$). The analysis is purely theoretical, using operator algebra and information-theoretic measures.
key_observables: Geometric Rényi divergence ($	ext{b}_{	ext{D}\alpha}$), Right Logarithmic Derivative (RLD) Fisher information ($	ext{bIF}$), and the mean-square error (MSE) in estimation.
important_parameters: The Rényi order $\alpha \in (0, 1) \cup (1, 2]$, the number of independent channels ($n$), and the parameter $	heta$ governing channel variation.
main_assumptions: The bounds are proven for deterministic processes satisfying a normalization requirement, and the Fisher information bound requires the channel families to be differentiable at the point of estimation.
paper_structure: The paper first develops the geometric Rényi divergence bound for non-definite causal order processes, then applies this framework to derive the additive bound for the RLD Fisher information, and finally discusses applications to channel discrimination and estimation.
why_interesting: The work provides fundamental, order-independent bounds for quantum resource quantification (like distinguishability and estimation precision), which is crucial for designing robust quantum protocols in realistic, non-sequential settings.

Figure 3: A capacity converse compares two experiments with the same process P and target test T. Resource channels produce ρ, which must pass with probability at least 1 −ε. Allowed comparison operations produce σ ∈S with Tr σ ≤1. Its unconditioned acceptance weight Tr(Tσ) is at most 2−ℓ. The process inequality bounds the divergence between these outputs. Preservation of S is an additional assumption on the complete communication protocol; it is not implied by deterministic normalization. The diagram is a comparison of experiments, not two stages of one protocol.
